title: The Political Economy of Protests in Iran
gist: Since 2017 every major Iranian protest wave except two has begun with economic grievances (inflation, currency collapse, fuel and food prices) and escalated into calls for regime change, met with ever-harsher repression by a leadership and IRGC that control vast parts of the economy; the December 2025-January 2026 uprising saw a record 7,000+ killed, followed by the US-Israel war from February 28, 2026, leaving a more hardline regime and conditions for renewed unrest.

insights.claim: Every major Iranian protest wave since 2017 (2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2025-26) was triggered by economic grievances such as inflation, currency devaluation, unemployment and fuel or food prices, and then spread nationwide with politicized regime-change slogans; only the hijab-related 2017-19 and 2022-23 movements were non-economic.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Iranian inflation and rial moves are leading indicators of unrest; monitor FX and price spikes for regime-stability risk.
insights.locator: Patterns of Economic Grievances

insights.claim: Iranians treat conservatives and reformists alike as responsible for the country's problems: presidential turnout fell from above 73 percent in 2017 to about 49 percent in 2021 and 40 percent in the first round of 2024, and protesters rejected President Pezeshkian's offers of dialogue.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Reformist-led easing offers little credibility; no domestic faction can easily defuse unrest through concessions.
insights.quote: Instead of voting, Iranians opted to organize and join periodic protests.
insights.locator: These recurring protests showed that the state suffered a serious legitimacy crisis

insights.claim: Protester composition has broadened from young working-class men to include merchants, professionals, the educated unemployed, slum residents and towns and villages, unlike the urban middle-class 2009 Green Movement.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Broader class base raises the threat level to the regime; bazaar participation is historically a regime-risk signal.
insights.locator: Demographically, from 2017 to 2026

insights.claim: When protests threaten the system, Iran's elites close ranks even if reformists voice criticism, so intra-elite factionalism does not produce a split that topples the regime.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Regime-collapse odds from elite splits remain low absent security-force defections.
insights.locator: At times, the protests, particularly those in 2017-2018, were provoked and exacerbated by intra-elite factionalism

insights.claim: Setad, a quasi-state organization under Khamenei's direct control with real estate, oil, telecom and finance assets, was estimated at $95 billion in 2013, and religious foundations (bonyad) under the supreme leader are estimated to control 20 to 50 percent of GDP with tax exemptions and no transparency.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Large parastatal monopolies crowd out the private sector and shape sanctions exposure and any post-regime economic restructuring.
insights.locator: Regime Repression and Economic Entanglement

insights.claim: The IRGC has become a multibillion dollar commercial empire with a stake estimated from 10 percent to over 50 percent of GDP, built through transfers of state-owned enterprises under Ahmadinejad, with its Khatam al-Anbiya construction headquarters a primary contractor for government projects in agriculture, infrastructure, mining, petroleum and transportation.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Entities tied to the IRGC span much of Iran's economy, so sanctions and post-war reconstruction exposure is widespread.
insights.locator: Under the guise of privatization and as stipulated by Article 44

insights.claim: Because the leader and IRGC protect their economic empires, repression is driven by wealth preservation as well as political power, and benefits of the 2015 JCPOA sanctions relief went to the state and parastatals under Khamenei instead of ordinary Iranians, whose poverty rate reached over 42 percent.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief would likely accrue to regime-linked entities first; limited trickle-down means relief does not reduce unrest risk quickly.
insights.locator: Dey Protests: 2017-2018

insights.claim: In September 2019 an Iranian parliamentarian claimed Khamenei and the IRGC controlled 60 percent of the economy through opaque entities, which reinforced public perceptions of corruption regardless of accuracy.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Perceived elite capture fuels protest legitimacy and corruption narratives (Iran scores 23 of 100 and ranks 151 of 180 on Transparency International).
insights.locator: Amid high inflation and other hardships

themes.theme: Prior protest cycles and macro data

insights.claim: The November 2019 fuel price hike raised gasoline prices 50 to 200 percent (10,000 rials per liter to 15,000 rials for the first 60 liters and 30,000 beyond), sparked protests in 100+ cities, and was followed by repression killing about 1,500 and more than 7,000 arrests per Iranian officials, plus a one-week internet blackout.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Fuel subsidy cuts are a proven flashpoint; any Iranian subsidy reform is high risk.
insights.locator: Bloody November or Aban Protests: 2019-2020

insights.claim: After Trump withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions on May 8, 2018, Iranian inflation rose from 9.7 percent to a high of 52 percent in May 2019, pushing an estimated 500,000 to 1.6 million Iranians into poverty.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Sanctions directly transmit into inflation and poverty, a template for current post-snapback conditions.
insights.locator: They worsened with Trump's withdrawal from the JCPOA

insights.claim: The Twelve-Day War in June 2025 caused roughly 40 percent currency devaluation and pushed inflation from 39.4 percent in June to 42.4 percent in August; after EU snapback sanctions in September 2025, inflation rose to 45.3 percent and then 48.6 percent in October.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Geopolitical shocks plus sanctions produced the macro backdrop for the 2025-26 uprising.
insights.locator: Recent Protests: 2025-2026

insights.claim: By December 2025 the rial hit a record low of 1.45 million per US dollar, food prices rose 72 percent and health and medical prices 50 percent, and merchants in Tehran's markets struck on December 27, including a conservative, state-friendly constituency that helped mobilize against the shah in 1979.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Merchant defection and currency collapse were the proximate triggers; watch the rial and bazaar strikes as stress indicators.
insights.locator: At the end of 2025, the snapback sanctions had been in place

insights.claim: The proposed budget aimed to raise taxes to cover a deficit from falling oil revenue caused by conflict and sanctions, while funding supreme leader and IRGC-linked foundations that already enjoy tax exemptions; merchants demanded a single exchange rate and tighter money supply controls.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Fiscal pressure from lost oil revenue pushes taxation onto merchants, a politically risky source of revenue.
insights.locator: Iranian merchants and shopkeepers also opposed the state's proposed budget

insights.claim: Pezeshkian's government responded to a historic drought by cutting electricity and water and considering evacuating the capital, and offered only $7 monthly payments and foreign-exchange subsidy reform that protesters dismissed as insufficient.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Water and power scarcity compounds economic grievances, adding environmental risk to Iran's stability outlook.
insights.locator: Before and during the protests, Iranians criticized Pezeshkian

insights.claim: Repression has escalated each cycle: about 20 deaths and 3,700 arrests in 2017-18; about 1,500 deaths and 7,000 arrests in 2019-20; at least 551 deaths and 19,262 arrests in 2022-23; and by February 15, 2026 at least 7,015 killed, 25,845 injured and 53,552 arrested in the 2025-26 protests per a human rights organization.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Rising lethality shows a regime prioritizing survival over concessions, with high probability of further violent crackdowns and executions (which doubled from 2024 to 2025).
insights.locator: Recent Protests: 2025-2026

insights.claim: In January 2026 the regime moved from disrupting to throttling the internet, used live ammunition, blinded hundreds or thousands by shooting at eyes, and reportedly recruited nearly 5,000 Iraqi Shia militia fighters paid $600 each, perhaps to reduce defection risk.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Reliance on foreign fighters signals concern about domestic security-force loyalty; defections are the key regime-change variable.
insights.locator: The regime's tactics this time were even more indiscriminate

insights.claim: Blackouts disrupted not only protests but also banks, businesses, hospitals and pharmacies, imposing an economic cost on the regime's own tactic.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Repeated shutdowns damage digital commerce and activity.
insights.locator: They were resigned to his inability to restrain the security forces

insights.claim: Trump's rhetoric that help was on the way, and the January 3 US capture of Venezuela's Maduro, emboldened Iranian protesters but also led the regime to see the protests as existential and crack down harder, while reinforcing its narrative that protesters were foreign agents.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: US signaling can raise repression intensity; external threats help the regime delegitimize dissent.
insights.locator: After the protests started, Trump attempted to exert greater pressure

insights.claim: In January the US evacuated Al Udeid and then backed off from attacking due to lack of preparedness; by late January and February Trump amassed the largest regional force since the 2003 Iraq invasion, including two carrier strike groups, while Gulf allies urged de-escalation and three rounds of talks were held in Oman and Geneva.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Shows the constraint set (Iranian missile deterrence, Gulf host-state fears, Hormuz risk) that preceded the war.
insights.locator: In late January and February, Trump amassed

insights.claim: Iran's deterrent options included drones and cruise and ballistic missiles that in the Twelve-Day War used up American and Israeli interceptors, and threatened closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of global oil and gas transits; Iran would likely close it only if regime survival were at stake.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Hormuz closure is the key energy-market tail risk; interceptor depletion is a constraint on US and Israeli operations.
insights.locator: The first was Iran's deterrence capability

insights.claim: The US and Israel went to war against Iran on February 28, 2026 and killed Khamenei and senior leaders on day one, yet the regime remained intact and became more hardline, militarized and securitized; Iran retaliated against the US, Israel and Gulf states and closed Hormuz to commercial traffic, raising petroleum prices.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Decapitation did not produce regime change; energy-price risk persists while the regime stays hostile.
insights.locator: Despite these risks and his promises to end America's so-called forever wars

insights.claim: The Assembly of Experts appointed Khamenei's son Mojtaba as supreme leader on March 8, and protesters changed their slogan to death to Mojtaba; the war killed 3,636 Iranians including at least 1,701 civilians by April 7, 2026 according to a human rights organization.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Dynastic succession under war conditions entrenches the security establishment.
insights.locator: After the Assembly of Experts appointed Khamenei's son Mojtaba

insights.claim: Reza Pahlavi remains a prominent figure with unclear organized support inside Iran and became more controversial by urging Iranians to risk their lives and by backing the US-Israeli war.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: No cohesive opposition alternative is evident, which lowers the probability of an organized transition.
insights.locator: Although Reza Pahlavi still seemed to have many supporters

insights.claim: The war and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports have worsened the inflation and currency collapse that sparked the protests, so the longer the conflict and the worse the economy, the greater the chance of renewed unrest.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Iran's economic deterioration under blockade is the leading indicator for renewed domestic instability.
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Billions of dollars of damage to schools, hospitals, power grids, communications, transport, oil installations and industrial plants, plus strikes on fuel depots and desalination plants, worsen air pollution and water insecurity, creating a post-war perfect storm of structural economic and environmental stress.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Reconstruction needs and water and power shortages are persistent drivers of instability and constrain Iranian oil and industrial output.
insights.quote: perfect storm of more periodic protests in the post-war phase
insights.locator: Even if high intensity hostilities do not restart soon

insights.claim: Absent substantive reform, the Islamic Republic will likely stay in a vicious cycle of mobilization and repression, and its survival through the war leaves it stronger in some ways, with the supreme leader's son supposedly in charge and newfound control of the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Eric Lob
insights.so_what: Base case is a durable, hardened regime with recurring unrest rather than collapse; Hormuz leverage keeps energy risk premia relevant.
insights.locator: All indications suggest the regime has not only survived the current conflict
